It proves that S'ântideva flourished in a period between the departure of I—Tsing from India in 695 and before S'ântarakṣita's first visit to Tibet in A. D. 743.²

### § 5 S'ântarakṣita's Style.

That S'ântarakṣita was an author of phenomenal learning is evident from every line of his writing. In almost every stanza he arranges the words in such a way that the minor term, major term, middle term and the example, invariably follow one after another is logical sequence. While stating the theories of his opponent he at once finds out from the amazing complications of the Indian philosophical literature the very essential grounds on which his theories are based, and states them one after another till the whole edifice is firmly established with all the fortifications of reasons and arguments. Thereafter he cunningly detects the broad and minute defects in the opponent's arguments and proceeds to attack the fort with the characteristic ability of an experienced tactician. He advances his arguments slowly and confidently, but with extraordinary caution, and with examples considered valid by both parties, anticipating objections which may be put forward by his antagonist at every step. These objections he nullifies as occasions arise, and ultimately smashes each and every argument on which the theories of his opponent are based, and drives his adversary to a corner. He then explains to his vanquished opponent what his position is tantamount to, and proves that the only way to escape from this undesirable position is to hold a Buddhist theory or be a Buddhist. On such occasions S'ântarakṣita is as jovial as a child and from his mouth flows examples of the very best kind of humour associated with a refined dignity. अविद्यमानसाध्यस्याभिमतः पदार्थ इति व्यापकानुपलब्धिः । एतच्च द्वयमपि प्रसङ्गसाधनमतो नोभयसिद्धोदाहरणेन किञ्चित् । यस्तु मन्यते साध्यः पुरुषस्यापि प्रतिबिम्बवन्न्यायेन भोगं प्रति कर्तृत्वमस्तीति । तं प्रत्येवं व्याचक्ष्माहे—मुक्त इत्यर्थः । यस्य हि मुक्तस्यापि भोगं प्रत्येव कर्तृत्वं नास्तीति नोदाहरणसिद्धिः ॥ १८ ॥

अथेत्यादिना परमतहेत्वोरसिद्धिमाशङ्कते ।

अथास्त्यतिशयः कश्चिदभिव्यक्त्यादिलक्षणः ।
यं हेतवः प्रकुर्वाणा न यान्ति वचनीयताम् ॥ १९ ॥

तत्र यदि प्रथमो हेतुः सर्वात्मनाऽभिव्यक्त्यादिरूपेणापि सत्त्वादिति सविशेषः क्रियते, तदा न सिद्ध्यति । न ह्यसामिरभिव्यक्त्यादिरूपेणापि सत्त्वमिष्यते कार्यस्य । किं तर्हि ? । शक्तिरूपेण । अथ सामान्येन निर्विशेषणस्तदाऽनैकान्तिकः, यस्मादभिव्यक्त्यादिलक्षणस्यातिशयस्योत्पद्यमानत्वात्, न सर्वस्य कार्यत्वप्रसङ्गो भविष्यति । अतएव द्वितीयोऽपि हेतुरसिद्धः, साध्यस्य विद्यमानत्वात् । अभिव्यक्त्यादिलक्षण इति । आदिशब्देनोद्रेकाद्यवस्थाविशेषपरिग्रहः । यमिति—अतिशयम् । वचनीयतामिति—वाच्यताम् । नामिमतो हेतुरसाध्यत्वादिलादिदोषो न भवतीति यावत् ॥ १९ ॥

प्रागासीदित्यादिना प्रतिविधत्ते—

प्रागासीद्यद्यसावेवं न किञ्चित्तमुत्तरम् ।
नो चेत्सोऽसत्कथं तेभ्यः प्रादुर्भावं समश्नुते ॥ २० ॥

तत्र विकल्पद्वयम्, कदाचिदसावतिशयोऽभिव्यक्त्याद्यवस्थातः प्राक् प्रकृतस्वभावामप्यासीद्वा न वा, यथासीत्तदा भवद्विद्वयोरपि हेत्वोर्न किञ्चित्सिद्धत्वादिकमुक्तमुत्तरम्, नो चेत्प्रागासीदेवमपि सोऽतिशयः कथं तेभ्यो हेतुभ्यः प्रादुर्भावमश्नुवीत, असदकारणादिति भवता न्यायान्न युक्तमेतदित्यभिप्रायः ॥ २० ॥

एवं तावदसत्करणादित्ययं हेतुः समर्थितः । साम्प्रतमुपादानपरिग्रहादित्यादिहेतुचतुष्टयसमर्थनार्थमाह—नातः साध्यमित्यादि ।

नातः साध्यं समस्तीति नोपादानपरिग्रहः ।
नियतादपि नो जन्म न च शक्तिर्न च क्रिया ॥ २१ ॥

यथोक्त्या नीत्या साध्यस्याभावादुपादानपरिग्रहो न प्राप्नोति, तत्साध्यफलानन्द-

[Whatever] does not have an existing object to be accomplished is the accepted substance <note>as a cause</note>; this is the non-perception of a universal. Neither of these two proofs is [invalid] by the example of something agreed upon by both. But he who thinks: "There is an object to be accomplished, as even the <term>puruṣa</term> has agency regarding experience, like a reflection"—we explain to him: [the <term>puruṣa</term>] is liberated, is the meaning. For the liberated one has no agency regarding experience, so the example is not proven. 18

With "Now," etc., he raises an objection regarding the non-proof of the two reasons of the opponent.

> Now, there is some surplus <note>attribute</note> characterized by manifestation and the like,
> which the causes, while producing, do not fall into being expressible <note>as having produced something new</note>. 19

In that case, if the first reason is qualified as "because it exists even in the form of manifestation," then it is not proven. For we do not accept that the effect exists even in the form of manifestation. What then? In the form of potentiality. Now, if it is general and unqualified, then it is uncertain, because a surplus characterized by manifestation and the like is being produced, so it will not follow that everything is an effect. Therefore, the second reason is also unproven, because the object to be accomplished <note>the surplus</note> exists. "Characterized by manifestation and the like"—by the word "etc.," special states such as intensity and the like are included. "Which"—the surplus. "Being expressible"—expressibility. The meaning is that the flaw such as "the cause is not accepted because it is not an object to be accomplished" does not occur. 19

With "Was it previously," etc., he refutes this.

> If that surplus was already there previously, then there is no answer to that.
> If not, how does it obtain manifestation from those causes? 20

There are two alternatives. Either that surplus existed in its own nature before the state of manifestation and the like, or it did not. If it existed, then there is no answer to the two reasons you stated, because nothing is proven. If it did not exist previously, then how could that surplus obtain manifestation from those causes? According to your own principle "because of non-production of the non-existent," this is not reasonable; this is the intent. 20

Thus, the reason "because of non-production of the non-existent" has been supported. Now, to support the four reasons starting with "because of the need for an underlying material," he says, "Therefore, an object," etc.

> Therefore, there is no object to be accomplished, so there is no need for an underlying material.
> There is no birth even from a fixed <note>cause</note>, and there is no potentiality and no action. 21

According to the stated logic, because there is no object to be accomplished, the need for an underlying material does not arise, as the intelligent would not accept it for the sake of the joy of the fruit of an object to be accomplished. The birth of curd and the like from a fixed cause like milk also does not hold, precisely because an object to be accomplished is impossible. This is the support for "because of the absence of all things being possible." Namely, "birth from a fixed cause" is spoken of precisely because of the absence of the possibility of birth from everything, and that is not reasonable in the theory of production of the existent because of the absence of an object to be accomplished. Similarly, the two—"producing what is capable" and "the nature of the cause"—are not reasonable. Precisely because of the absence of an object to be accomplished. If something were to be completed by someone, then the potentiality of the completed thing would be established. And the production of what is to be completed would be proven. Not otherwise. He shows this with "and no potentiality and no action." 21

<summary>The author continues to dismantle the Sāṃkhya theory of causality by arguing that without an "object to be accomplished," the supporting pillars of their system—such as underlying material, fixed causality, and potentiality—collapse.</summary>
<keywords>causality, Sāṃkhya, production, potentiality, logic</keywords>

न्यापोढ इत्युच्यते । वेनापोहः शब्दार्थ इति प्रसिद्धम् । तत्र विधिवादिनश्चोदयन्ति । यदि भवतां द्रव्यगुणकर्मसामान्यविशेषसमवायलक्षणा उपाधयो विशेषणानि शब्दप्रत्ययं प्रति निमित्तानि परमार्थतो न सन्ति, तत्कथं लोके दण्डीत्यभिधानप्रत्ययाः प्रवर्तन्ते द्रव्याद्युपाधिनिमित्ताः । तथाहि—दण्डी विपाणीत्यादिधीध्वनी लोके द्रव्योपाधिकौ प्रसिद्धौ, शुक्लः कृष्ण इति गुणोपाधिकौ, चलति भ्रमतीति कर्मनिमित्तौ, अस्ति विद्यत इति सत्ताप्रवृत्तिनिमित्तकौ, गौरश्वो हस्तीति सामान्यविशेषोपाधी, इह तन्तुषु पट इति समवायवलात् । तत्रैषां द्रव्यादीनामभावे दण्डीत्यादिधीध्वनी निर्विषयौ स्यातामिति । आदिग्रहणं प्रत्येकमभिसम्बध्यते । तेन प्रत्येकं छत्री विपाणीत्यादिसमानजातीयधीध्वनीनां ग्रहणं भवति । अन्यास्तु विशेषा योगिनामेव ग्राह्या इति न तेषामादिशब्देन परिग्रहः । न चानिमित्तत्वेतौ युक्तौ, सर्वत्राविशेषेण सर्वदा तयोर्वृत्तिप्रसङ्गात् । न चाविभागेन तयोः प्रवृत्तिरस्ति । तस्मात्सन्ति द्रव्यादय इति परः । प्रयोगः—ये परस्परमसङ्कीर्णप्रवृत्तयस्ते सनिमित्ताः, यथा श्रोत्रादिप्रत्ययाः, असङ्कीर्णप्रवृत्तयश्च दण्डीत्यादिशब्दप्रत्यया इति स्वभावहेतुः । अनिमित्तत्वे सर्वत्राविशेषेण प्रवृत्तिप्रसङ्गो बाधकं प्रमाणम् ॥ ८६७ ॥ ८६८ ॥

उच्यत इत्यादिना प्रतिविधत्ते ।
> उच्यते विपयोऽमीषां धीध्वनीनां न कश्चन ।
> अन्तर्मात्रानिविष्टं तु बीजमेषां निबन्धनम् ॥ ८६९ ॥

तत्र यदि मुख्यतो बाह्येन विषयभूतेन सनिमित्तत्वमेषां साधयितुमिष्टं तदाऽनैकान्तिकता हेतोः साध्यविपर्यये बाधकप्रमाणाभावात् । अथ येन केनचिन्निमित्तेन सनिमित्तत्वमिष्यते तदा सिद्धसाध्यता । तथा हस्माभिरिष्यत एवापमन्तर्जल्पवासनाप्रबोधो निमित्तम्, न तु विषयभूतं, भ्रान्तत्वेन पूर्वस्य शाब्दप्रत्ययस्य निर्विषयत्वात् । अन्तर्मात्रानिविष्टमिति । विज्ञानसन्निविष्टं, वासनेति यावत् ॥ ८६९ ॥

एतदेवागमेन संस्पन्दयन्नाह—यस्य यस्येत्यादि ।
> यस्य यस्य हि शब्दस्य यो यो विषय उच्यते ।
> स स (संविद्य)ते नैव वस्तूनां सा हि धर्मता ॥ ८७० ॥

यो यो विषय इति । स्वलक्षणसामान्यादिः । सा हि धर्मतेति । सा—प्रकृतिः, सर्ववाक्पथातीतत्वं वस्तूनां स्वभाव इति यावत् । यथोक्तम्—"येन येन हि नाम्ना वै यो यो धर्मोऽभिलप्यते । न स संविद्यते तत्र धर्माणां सा हि धर्मते"ति ॥ ८७० ॥

<header>Together with the Pañjikā</header>

...and because it is the result of achieving the object of <term>apoha</term> <gloss>exclusion</gloss>, it is said that <term>apoha</term> is the meaning of the word. The advocates of affirmation object: if the attributes such as substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence, which are the causes for verbal expressions and cognitions, do not exist in reality, then how do verbal expressions and cognitions in the world, which are caused by substance and other attributes, operate? Specifically, the cognition and word "staff-bearer" and "having horns" are known in the world to be caused by the attribute of substance; "white" and "black" by the attribute of quality; "moves" and "wanders" by the attribute of action; "exists" and "is" by the attribute of existence; "cow," "horse," and "elephant" by the attributes of generality and particularity; and "the cloth is in the threads" by the power of inherence. There, in the absence of these substances and so on, the cognition and word "staff-bearer" and so on would be without an object. The word "ādi" <gloss>and so on</gloss> applies to each; thus, it includes the grasping of similar kinds of cognitions and words like "umbrella-bearer" and "having horns." Other particulars are to be grasped only by yogis, so they are not included by the word "ādi." And it is not reasonable for these to be without a basis, as it would follow that they could be applied everywhere without distinction and at all times. And there is no operation of them without distinction. Therefore, substance and so on exist. The argument: those whose operations are not confused with each other have a basis, like the cognitions of the ear, and the words and cognitions such as "staff-bearer" are not confused in their operations. This is a nature-based reason. In the absence of a basis, the consequence of applying them everywhere without distinction is the proving contradiction. 867-868

He replies with "It is said," etc.

> It is said that there is no object at all for these cognitions and words. 
> The seed of these, which is contained only within, is the basis. 869

If it is intended to prove that these have a basis in an external object as the primary domain, then the reason is indecisive because there is no contradictory evidence to the negation of what is to be proved. If they are intended to have a basis in any cause whatsoever, then it is a case of proving what is already proved. We do indeed intend the awakening of the latent impressions of internal chatter to be the cause, not an external object, since the previous verbal cognition is objectless due to being erroneous. "Contained only within"—meaning contained in consciousness, which is what "latent impression" <term>vāsanā</term> means. 869

He confirms this with scripture by saying: "Of whom," etc.

> Whatever object is said for any word, 
> that object does not exist at all in things; that is the nature of things. 870

"Whatever object"—meaning the individual trait <term>svalakṣaṇa</term>, the generality, etc. "That is the nature of things"—that is the intrinsic state, meaning that the nature of things is to be beyond all paths of speech. As it is said: "Whatever property is spoken of by whatever name, that does not exist there; that is the nature of properties." 870

न ह्यवस्तुनो भेदो युक्तो वस्त्वधिष्ठानत्वात्तस्य । तस्मादभावो वस्तु । कीदृशं पुनरस्य वस्तुत्वमित्याह--कार्यादीनामिति । क्षीरादेः कारणस्य यो भावः स एव दध्यादेः कार्यस्याभावः, कार्यस्य दध्यादेर्भावः स एव क्षीरादेः कारणस्याभाव इत्येतदभाववस्तुत्वम् ॥ १६५५ ॥

पुनरप्यनुमानेन वस्तुत्वमस्य प्रतिपादयन्नाह--यद्वेत्यादि ।

यद्वानुवृत्तिव्यावृत्तिबुद्धयोर्गम्यो यतः स्वयम् ।
तस्माद्वादिषद्वस्तु प्रमेयत्वाच्च गम्यताम् ॥ १६५६ ॥

अभावो यस्त्विति पक्षः, अनुवृत्तिव्यावृत्तिबुद्धित्वात्प्रमेयत्वाच्चेति हेतुद्वयं, गवादिवदिति दृष्टान्तः ॥ १६५६ ॥

तत्रानुवृत्तिबुद्धिरुपलभ्यमानभावोऽभाव इत्येषाकारः प्रत्ययः । व्यावृत्तिबुद्धिः प्रागभावोऽयं न प्रध्वंसाभाव इत्यादिभेदाकारः प्रत्ययः । तत्र कुमारिलेन त्रिविधोऽभावो वर्णितः । आत्मनोऽपरिणाम एकः, पदार्थान्तरविशेषज्ञानं द्वितीयः, "माऽऽत्मनोऽपरिणामो वा विशानं वाऽन्यवस्तुनो"ति वचनात्, प्रमाणनिवृत्तिमात्रमात्मस्तृतीयः; त्रिलक्षणेन या बुद्धिर्जन्यते साऽनुमेप्यते । "नपानुवृत्तिरूपस्य कारणाधीनता वचि"दिति वचनात् । तत्रैतस्मिस्तृतीयेऽभावे दोषमाश्रित्य परिहरन्नाह--मानं कथमभावश्चेदिति ।

मानं कथमभावश्चेत्प्रमेयं चात्र कीदृशम् ।
मेयो यद्वदभावो हि मानमप्येषमिष्यताम् ॥ १६५७ ॥

अथोच्यते कथं प्रमाणानुत्पत्तिलक्षणोऽभावः प्रमाणमिति । अत्रोच्यते--प्रमेयं चात्र कीदृशमिति । अभाव रूपं प्रमेयंमिति चेत् । एवं तर्हि यथाभूतं प्रमेयं तथाभूतमेव प्रमाणमितिष्यताम् । यत्तु युज्यते--मानं कथमभाव इति । यदि तन्न प्रमाणं (न) युक्तम् ॥ १६५७ ॥

भवत्वभावः प्रमाणं प्रमाणदिष्वेषु भेदोऽस्य कथमित्याह--अभायेत्यादि ।

अभावशब्दावाच्यत्वादात्मलक्षादेश विश्रमे ।
प्रमाणानामभावो हि प्रमेयाणाममापयत् ॥ १६५८ ॥
अभावो वा प्रमाणेन गानुरूपेण मीयते ।
प्रमेयत्वाद्यथाऽऽत्मज्ञानात्प्रमाणत्वम् ॥ १६५९ ॥

It is not logical for a non-object to have divisions, because its basis is an object. Therefore, absence is an object. What kind of objectivity is this? He says: "Of effects, etc." The existence of the cause, like milk, is the absence of the effect, like curd; the existence of the effect, like curd, is the absence of the cause, like milk—this is the objectivity of absence. 1655

Again, establishing its objectivity by inference, he says: "Or," etc.

> Or, because it is knowable by the cognitions of continuation and exclusion,
> Therefore, like a cow, etc., let it be known as an object due to being knowable. 1656

Absence is the subject; "because it is cognitions of continuation and exclusion" and "due to being knowable" are the two reasons; "like a cow, etc." is the example. 1656

There, the cognition of continuation is a perception in the form of "an existing being is perceived as absent." The cognition of exclusion is a perception in the form of distinctions such as "this is prior absence, not posterior absence." Kumārila described three types of absence. One is the non-transformation of the self; the second is the cognition of another object, according to the statement: "Either the non-transformation of the self or the consciousness of another object"; the third is merely the cessation of a means of knowledge. The cognition produced by the three-fold characteristics is inferred. According to the statement: "The form of continuation is not dependent on causes anywhere." Addressing the flaw in this third type of absence, he replies: "If absence is a means of knowledge, how?"

> If absence is a means of knowledge, then what is the object to be known here?
> If absence is the object to be known, then let it be granted that it is also a means of knowledge. 1657

If it is said: How is absence, defined as the non-origination of a means of knowledge, a means of knowledge? To this, he says: "And what is the object to be known here?" If you say absence is the object to be known, then let the object to be known be the same as the means of knowledge. What is logical is: how is absence a means of knowledge? If it is not a means of knowledge, then it is not logical. 1657

Let absence be a means of knowledge; how is it distinguished from the other means of knowledge? He says: "By the word absence," etc.

> Due to being expressed by the word absence, in resting on the self-nature, etc.,
> The absence of means of knowledge is indeed the non-measuring of objects to be known. 1658
> Or absence is measured by a means of knowledge corresponding to itself.
> Because it is an object to be known, like knowledge of the self, it has the status of a means of knowledge. 1659

# रत्नावली

## भूमिका

१९वीं सदी के अन्तिम पाद से लेकर २०वीं सदी के पूर्वाद्ध तक का समय भारतीय संस्कृति के तत्त्वों के अन्वेषण का महत्त्वपूर्ण समय कहा जा सकता है । इसी अवधि में भारत को फिर से अपनी उन अमूल्य निधियों का पता चला जो उसकी दृष्टि से तिरोहित हो चुकी थीं । वैदिक संस्कृति के ग्रन्थों का कभी भी भारत की भूमि से आमूल लोप नहीं हुआ, इसलिए सामान्य रूप से उसके ग्रन्थ परम्परया सुरक्षित रहे । परन्तु बारहवीं सदी में अनेक कारणों के सम्मिलित आघात को सहन नहीं कर बौद्धधर्म और दर्शन को भारत के बाहर केवल उत्तरी देशों में ही शरण मिली । भारत से वस्तुतः बौद्धधर्म का लोप हो गया । ऐसी स्थिति में बौद्ध-विचार का परिचय केवल प्रतिपक्षियों के कथन के आधार पर ही प्राप्त कर सन्तोष करना पड़ता था । जो भी कुछ उद्धृत अंश यत्र-तत्र उपलब्ध होते थे वे आंशिकतः अथवा मूल के विपर्यस्त रूप के कारण यथार्थ मत का प्रतिनिधित्व नहीं करते थे । यह स्थिति तब तक बनी रही जब तक बौद्ध-दर्शन के मूलग्रन्थ भारत में उपलब्ध नहीं हो पाए थे । जब पाश्चात्य मनीषियों की अभिरुचि बौद्ध दर्शन में हुई तो उनके प्रयासों से नेपाल, तिब्बत और चीन से बहुत-से दुर्लभ

# Ratnavali
# <note>Precious Garland</note>

## Introduction

The period from the final quarter of the 19th century to the first half of the 20th century can be called a significant time for the exploration of the elements of Indian culture. During this period, India once again discovered those invaluable treasures that had disappeared from its sight. The texts of Vedic culture never completely vanished from the land of India, so generally, those texts remained preserved through tradition. However, in the 12th century, unable to withstand the combined impact of various causes, Buddhism and its philosophy found refuge outside of India, primarily in northern countries. Buddhism effectively vanished from India. In such a situation, one had to be satisfied with gaining an introduction to Buddhist thought based only on the statements of its opponents. Whatever quoted portions were available here and there did not represent the true view because they were either partial or represented a distorted version of the original. This situation persisted until the original texts of Buddhist philosophy became available in India. When Western scholars developed an interest in Buddhist philosophy, many rare

<note>original: "मनीषियों" refers to learned scholars or thinkers.</note>

manuscripts were brought from Nepal, Tibet, and China through their efforts and subsequently published.

शरीरतापनं धर्मः केवलान्नास्ति तेन हि ।
नं परद्रोहविरतिर्न परेषामनुग्रहः ॥ ११ ॥
शरीर को केवल सताने से ही धर्म नहीं होता है । इसलिए न तो ( स्कन्ध आदि ) सापेक्ष वस्तुओं के साथ द्वेषभाव को बिल्कुल छोड़ देना चाहिए और न उन पर कृपा ही करनी चाहिए ॥ ११ ॥

दानशीलक्षमास्पष्टं यः सद्धर्ममहापथम् ।
अनादृत्य व्रजेत् कायक्लेशगो दण्डकोत्पथैः ॥ १२ ॥
जो शरीर कष्ट देने वाला व्यक्ति दान, शील और क्षमा से प्रशस्त सच्चे धर्म ( = बौद्ध धर्म ) के महान् मार्ग का अनादर कर दण्ड के उन्मार्ग से चलता है ॥ १२ ॥

स संसारवीं घोरमनन्तजनपादपाम् ।
क्लेशव्यालावलीढाङ्गः सुदीर्घं प्रतिपद्यते ॥ १३ ॥
वह क्लेशरूपी सर्प से अपने अंग को डँसवाता हुआ अनगिनत मनुष्य रूपी वृक्षों से युक्त संसार के निविड जंगल में बहुत समय तक भटकता है ॥ १३ ॥

हिंसाया जायतेऽल्पायुः वङ्गाबाधो विहिंसया ।
चौर्येण भोगव्यसनी सशत्रुः पारदारिकः ॥ १४ ॥
हिंसा से आयु घटती है और निर्दयता से अनेक प्रकार के कष्ट होते हैं । चोरी से भोग में व्यसन होता है और परस्त्री के प्रति आसक्त व्यक्ति शत्रुवान् होता है ॥ १४ ॥

प्रत्याख्यानं मृषावादात् पैशुन्यान्निन्नभेदनम् ।
अप्रियश्रवणं शैक्ष्यादपार्थं दुर्भंगं वचः ॥ १५ ॥
मिथ्याकथन से ( सत्य का ) निराकरण होता है, चुगलखोरी से

Dharma does not exist merely by tormenting the body. Therefore, one should neither completely abandon nor show favor to the <note>skandha-like</note> relative objects with hatred [11].

He who, ignoring the great path of true Dharma (Buddhism) adorned with charity, conduct, and patience, walks on the evil path of punishment by tormenting the body [12].

He wanders for a very long time in the dense forest of the world, which is filled with countless trees of human life, while his limbs are bitten by the serpent of suffering <term>klesha</term> [13].

Violence leads to a short life, and cruelty leads to many types of suffering. Theft leads to addiction to sense-pleasures, and a person attached to another's wife gains enemies [14].

Lying leads to the rejection of truth, slander leads to the breaking of friendships, harsh speech leads to hearing unpleasant things, and meaningless speech leads to unfortunate words [15].

( ५३ )

नपुंसक राजगण मनोरथों से भी जिसकी क्षति नहीं पहुँचा सके हैं ऐसे तीनों रत्नों के आश्रय को श्रीमान् (= बुद्ध ) द्वारा कथित धर्म का स्थान बनाओ ॥ १० ॥

सामन्तराजरोमाञ्च करं धर्मस्पदं न यत् ।
मृतस्याप्यप्रशस्तत्वाद् राजस्तदकृतं वरम् ॥ ११ ॥
सामन्त और राजाओं को रोमाञ्चित करने वाला जो धर्म का आश्रय नहीं है, वह मरे हुए के लिए भी हेय है । इसलिए, हे राजन् ! उसे न करना अच्छा है ॥ ११ ॥

अत्यौदार्यादुदाराणां विस्मयोत्साहवर्धनम् ।
उत्साहघ्नं च मन्दानां सर्वस्वेनापि कारय ॥ १२ ॥
अत्यन्त उदारता के द्वारा उदार व्यक्तियों के उत्साह को खूब बढ़ाओ । मूखों के उत्साह की हानि सब कुछ अर्पित करके भी करवाओ ॥ १२ ॥

उत्सृज्यामुत्र गन्तव्यं सर्वस्वमवशेन ते ।
धर्मे नियुक्तं यात्येव पुरस्तात्सर्वमेव तत् ॥ १३ ॥
तुम्हारे बिना वश के सब कुछ छोड़कर तुम्हें परलोक जाना है । ( परन्तु ) धर्म में जो लगाओगे वह सब तुम्हारे आगे-आगे जाएगा ही ॥ १३ ॥

सर्वस्वं पूर्वनृपतेर्नपस्य वशमागतम् ।
किं पूर्वकस्य धर्माय सुखाय यशसेऽपि वा ॥ १४ ॥
अतीतकाल के राजा का सारा धन वर्त्तमानकाल के राजा के वश में आ गया । क्या पहले के राजा का धन उसके धर्म, सुख या यश के लिए भी हुआ ? ॥ १४ ॥

भुक्तादर्थादिह सुखं दत्तात्पारत्रिकं सुखम् ।
अभुक्तादत्तनष्टत्वाद् दुःखमेव कुतः सुखम् ॥ १५ ॥
भोग किए हुए धन से इस लोक में सुख होता है और दान किए हुए धन से परलोक में सुख होता है । जिसका भोग नहीं किया गया,

( 53 )

Whatever is not an abode of <term>dharma</term> that makes feudal lords and kings thrill with excitement is disparaged even after one's death. Therefore, O King, it is better not to do such things. [11]

Through great generosity, heighten the wonder and enthusiasm of the generous. Even by sacrificing everything, cause the loss of enthusiasm among the foolish. [12]

You must go to the next world leaving everything behind against your will. However, all that you invest in <term>dharma</term> will go ahead of you. [13]

The entire wealth of a past king has come under the control of the current king. Did the wealth of the previous king result in his <term>dharma</term>, happiness, or fame? [14]

Wealth that is enjoyed brings happiness in this world, and wealth that is given brings happiness in the next. Wealth that is neither enjoyed nor given, but is lost, brings only suffering. Where is the happiness in that? [15]

## *A short note on the Avadána Kalpalatá.*

The first forty chapters of the *Avadána Kalpalatá* were lost in India for several centuries. In the Hodgson and Wright Collections of Buddhist Sanskrit MSS., brought from Nepal, the remaining chapters only of that work were available; and in one of the MSS. of it there is a passage to the effect that, though searched for very carefully, the first part is nowhere to be found (पूर्वाद्धं कुत्रचिन्न प्राप्तम्).

Under these circumstances the announcement of the recovery of the complete work from Tibet, with its Tibetan translation, was received with pleasure by the Asiatic Society of Bengal, and the Council gave permission to publish it with the translation, for the purpose of facilitating the study of the classical Tibetan through the medium of Sanskrit.

The materials used for the preparation of this edition cannot therefore be expected to be very ample. The Sanskrit original is a block print from Lhasa written in Tibetan characters. The blocks are upwards of two hundred years old. In some places the impressions are not very distinct, and the blocks, having been prepared at a place so far away from the seat of Sanskrit learning, cannot be expected to be as correct as might be desired. The MSS. used in the preparation of the blocks had not been altogether free from defects, as has been acknowledged twice in the footnotes of the Tibetan translation of the second *pallava*. In one place a verse was wanting, and its place was supplied by another by re-translating the Tibetan word for word, and in another a line was wanting which has been similarly replaced. The occurrence of slight discrepancies of spelling and grammar in the block-print is therefore not to be wondered at. Where the Sanskrit gives no sense, the translation is a great help. The translation has been very carefully made; and in ascertaining the meaning of difficult passages, its utility has been very great. The Buddhist Sanskrit, it is well-known, differs from the classical Sanskrit of Páṇini in many respects, both in grammar and dictionary, and the knowledge of Buddhist Sanskrit may be said to be still in its infancy. I have not therefore ventured to make alterations in the text to suit the requirements of classical Sanskrit. I have noted in the footnotes all those cases in which I have been obliged to make slight alterations in the text to suit the meaning as given in the translation. A list of those cases in which, apart from evident clerical errors and slips, some changes might have been made either in spelling or in grammar to conform to the rules of ordinary Sanskrit, is subjoined. The reason for not making these changes in the published text is, that some of them come within the scope of options given in Sanskrit grammar and orthography, though such options are seldom availed of by classical writers, and also that some of them may prove with the progress of Buddhist Sanskrit studies to be true Buddhistic forms.

HARIMOHAN SARMA.

# The Third Chapter

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

You have acted of your own accord, with a conduct that is indifferent to your own needs, even regarding your own life, for the sake of those who seek help. This body, which is like a cluster of lotuses, has been willingly placed by you in a position of destruction. 178

O King, is there any desire for a reward in this vow of virtue, even as you wager your very life? Does your mind not suffer any distress from the pain of your palate being split for the sake of this petitioner? 179

Thus was he questioned by the sage, whose mind was filled with wonder, in the midst of the great ascetics. The King, having wiped his face which was drenched in blood, restrained his pain with great effort and spoke: 180

O Sage, I have no other desire for a reward, but there is one great longing: that I may exist in every birth solely for the purpose of rescuing living beings who are submerged in the terrifying cycle of worldly existence <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</gloss>. 181

<summary>The King is questioned by a sage regarding his selfless sacrifice and explains that his only motivation is the liberation of all suffering beings from the cycle of rebirth.</summary>
<keywords>sacrifice, compassion, samsara, rebirth, virtue, Buddhist ethics, King, sage</keywords>

བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོའི་བློ་གྲོས་ནི། སྨན་པ་འབྲལ་བས་མ་ཡིན་ཞིང་། །

# Sixth Chapter <note>original: ཡལ་འདབ་དྲུག་པ།, literally "Sixth Leaf" or "Sixth Branch"</note>

Again, having boarded a ship, he completely crossed the ocean <note>original: ཆུ་བོའི་གཏེར་, literally "treasure of waters"</note>. From the slopes of the Jewel Mountain, he entered into a dense forest. 123

The intellect of the Great Soul <note>original: བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་, Sanskrit: Mahatma</note> was not separated from the role of a healer. He did not act through affliction, hostile sorcery, disease, or the practice of emotional taints. 124

There, he saw a mountain that reached into the sky, blocking every direction without exception. Like a physical obstacle standing before him, it was difficult to traverse. 125

Seeing that mountain which acted like a source of delusion, his means became diminished. He lay down upon a mat made of leaves and reflected for a moment: 126

"Alas! Since I entered this path, how much time has passed in the interval? I have not even heard the name of the Island of <term>Badara</term> <gloss>a mythical island or place of jujube trees</gloss> with any certainty." 127

"My merit <note>original: བསོད་ནམས་, Sanskrit: punya</note> is exhausted. That which was the supreme companion of my diligence has been broken by the power of karma, like a mast snapping at the wrong time." 128

"Even though my means are failing, through this very great effort, I shall certainly never turn back. I will either achieve success or I will die." 129

"In these three worlds, the one whose life is exhausted for the sake of benefiting others is the only one worthy of being honored among living beings." 130

<summary>The protagonist crosses the ocean and faces a massive mountain obstacle while searching for the Island of Badara. He resolves to either succeed in his altruistic quest or die trying, emphasizing the value of self-sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Mahatma, Jewel Mountain, Badara Island, merit, karma, altruism, perseverance</keywords>

pages.translation:
# Tenth Chapter <note>original: Dashama Pallava</note>

Alas, my beloved! Like a deceitful gambler who has abandoned the truth, I have observed this false vow only to steal your heart. 46

I shall abandon this vow at once and go to the side of my dear one. For those burning with passion, the heat of penance is truly unbearable. 47

When the princess sees me, the cruel one who has been away for so long, I do not know what she will do in her newly sparked resentment. 48

A painful insult to love does not always lead to a change of heart; a speck of dust dissolved in oil <note>referring to the "sneha" or oil of affection</note> becomes impossible to remove. 49

The very moment I see the forest is empty of the Blessed One <note>referring to the Buddha</note>, I must go home; this is my firm resolve. 50

On this very stone slab, using beautiful mountain minerals, I shall paint that moon-faced woman to find a support for my fortitude. 51

Or rather, how can my beloved ever become a subject for a painting? The drops of her beauty are like nectar, blue water-lilies, and the moon itself. 52

Her gaze possesses the movement of a startled deer and the flickering of bees or black snakes in the heart of a lotus. The radiance of her lips is like a forest of coral on the shore of the ocean of loveliness. Her facial splendor is the refuge for the entire collection of faultless moonbeams. How can such a body, the very essence of wonder, ever be captured in a painting? 53

<summary>A lover expresses deep regret over his ascetic vows and decides to return to his beloved princess. He contemplates painting her likeness on a stone but concludes that her divine beauty is too great for any artistic representation.</summary>
<keywords>longing, asceticism vs love, painting, beauty, Sanskrit poetry, Kavya, Buddha, devotion</keywords>

For the character <term>Shou</term> <gloss>beast</gloss>, the fanqie <note>a system of indicating pronunciation by using two characters</note> is 'chou' and 'shu', reversed. The dictionary says it means to herd. The *Guoyu* <note>Discourses of the States</note> says "beast" means a group. The *Zilin* <note>Forest of Characters</note> says it is pronounced 'chou' and 'shu'. In the sutra text, the character 'hang' <gloss>row/path</gloss> is used. For 'ji', the fanqie is 'li' and 'zhong', meaning "sovereign." The *Record of Rites* says it refers to winter hunting, but that is not the meaning here; it refers to domestic animals. Ancient texts mention catching dragons; if one cannot tame them, how can one catch them? For 'ji', the fanqie is 'you', referring to a water deity. The *Kaosheng* <note>Examination of Sounds</note> says 'ji' means to gather, referring to still water. The character 'du' <gloss>cabinet/case</gloss> is composed of 'mu' <gloss>wood</gloss>. The *Erya* <note>Approaching Elegance</note> says 'ji' <gloss>female animal</gloss> is the child of 'ji'. Guo's commentary says that today the female of a green-headed ox is called 'pin', which is formed with the 'niu' <gloss>ox</gloss> radical.
For 'pi' <gloss>comb</gloss>, the fanqie is 'bian' and 'fen'. The *Kaosheng* says it is a bamboo tool for moving things.
'Mo' <gloss>to touch</gloss> means to rub. For 'cheng', the fanqie is 'hua' and 'fan'. The three parts refer to the palm and the thumb, both called 'zhang' <gloss>palm</gloss>. The sutra says:
<column-break/>
The "eight" refers to the three sweet substances. For 'tian' <gloss>sweet</gloss>, the fanqie is 'die' and 'jian'. The dictionary says it means delicious or sweet. One word is 'ding-weng-zhi-li' <note>a transliteration of a foreign term</note>. The King's Sutra says the three sweet substances are ghee, milk, and curd, which are highly valued in the Western Regions. For 'ji-zhu' <gloss>loom shuttle</gloss>, the fanqie for 'ji' is 'ju' and 'yi', and for 'zhu' is 'chu' and 'zu'. The *Fangyan* <note>Regional Dialects</note> says it is a tool for weaving.

The commentary on the <term>Xiang</term> of the <term>Tai</term> <gloss>Peace hexagram</gloss> says: "Peace: the small departs, the large arrives. This is auspicious and successful." This means that Heaven and Earth communicate, and all things flourish. The upper and lower communicate, and their wills are the same. "Upper and lower" refers to the inner presence of the positive <term>yang</term> and the outer presence of the negative <term>yin</term>; the inner is vigorous, the outer is compliant; the inner is the noble man, the outer is the small man. The way of the noble man grows, and the way of the small man fades.

Your subject observes: Heaven is high and Earth is low, which establishes their positions; ruler and subject are inferior and superior, which establishes their order. If there is no communication of energy and will, then they are suspended in separation and do not connect; they are discordant and not united. In an age of peace where there is communication, the ruler and subjects are virtuous, the masses are harmonious and in accord, and the small men are reformed. Between the superior and the inferior, there is kindness and sincerity, bound together so tightly they cannot be separated. This is what is meant by saying that while their ranks are distinct, the affection between ruler and subject is like that of father and son.

# Imperial-Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries

The events can be examined without needing to explicitly demote or reject them; the evil reveals itself naturally. Duke Xuan reigned for nine years, during which he went to Zhou only once to pay respects, yet he went to Qi to pay court twice. The *Annals* severely blames him for going to Qi without first fulfilling his duty to the king.

The subject observes: The Duke of Lu personally paid court to a neighboring state but ordered a high official to pay respects at the imperial capital. The capital received only one visit, while Qi received two or three. This is like reversing the order of things, asserting that the dignity of one’s father is inferior to that of one’s elder brother. This is even worse than the case of Gongzi Sui going to the imperial capital and then to Jin. This is how the *Spring and Autumn Annals* records these events to rectify the ethics of ruler and subject.

In autumn, the Heavenly King, Ding, sent Wang Jizi to pay a visit.

Your servant submits: The meaning of "respecting one's person" is rooted in the "Duke Ai Questions the Master" chapter of the <term>Liji</term> <gloss>Record of Rites</gloss>. The Master’s words explain the <term>Liji</term> by using the classic text's principle—that those who love their parents dare not hate others, and those who respect their parents dare not show contempt for others—as evidence. Zhen Dexiu’s words further cite the language used when parents provide the marriage cap for a son or send off a daughter to substantiate this meaning. It is intended to make one mindful of the teachings of one's parents. If one is ever disrespectful, then one commits a sin against one's parents. Thus, there will never be a time when there is negligence in the mutual respect between husband and wife. The above is the essence of the Way of husband and wife.

...as wind, speaking in terms of <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy</gloss>. When it is on the earth, it is wood, speaking in terms of material substance. Regarding the images of <term>Kan</term>, in <term>Tun</term> and <term>Xu</term> it speaks of clouds; clouds are what water rises into. In <term>Meng</term> it speaks of springs; springs are the source of water. In <term>Xie</term> it speaks of rain; rain is what water descends as. Regarding the images of <term>Li</term>, in its own hexagram it speaks of brilliance; in <term>Jin</term> and <term>Mingyi</term> it speaks of brilliance. Brilliance is the function of fire; therefore, the sun is called "Great Brilliance." In <term>Shihe</term> and <term>Feng</term> it speaks of thunder and lightning, which is the splendor of fire in the sky. Regarding the images of <term>Dui</term>, in its aspect of marshes it speaks of water; it is where water gathers. When the <term>Yi</term> forms images, it proceeds from the subtle to the manifest. Thunder and wind are images without physical form. Water and fire are images with physical form. Mountain and lake are images with physical shape. # PREFACE.

---

In issuing this last volume of the Aṅguttara-Nikāya I have to say a few words on the work now laid before the public in a complete edition¹.

It was in spring 1896 that I began transcribing and collating those parts of the Aṅguttara which were left unfinished by the lamented Dr. Richard Morris, and in autumn 1898 I had finished my transcript and collation of the eleventh Nipāta. For the whole work, from Part III—V, I have had the same five MSS. which have been spoken of by me in the Preface to Part III, *sub* 1—5. These MSS. are identical with those which Dr. Morris made use of in Parts I and II of his edition, respectively. Moreover, I have gone fully into the Siamese edition, and, for some parts of the sixth Nipāta, and for the whole of the seventh and eighth Nipātas I had at my disposal another MS., mentioned *sub* 6 in the Preface noticed before. I am sorry I was not able to mention two further MSS., likewise consulted by my hon. predecessor, but only for Part I, because these MSS. belong to the Collection of Pāli MSS. in the British Museum, and it was impossible for me to make a longer stay in London to collate them.

If we are to judge from our MSS., we may fairly assume three different versions of the Aṅguttara, a Sinhalese, a Burmese, and a Siamese, the last being represented only by the edition of the present King of Siam, this last,

---

¹ See, besides, the Preliminary Remarks to Parts I and II, by the Rev. Dr. Morris.

<header>VII.1—3 Ānisamsa-Vagga. 9</header>

"no perception of the sphere of boundless consciousness in the sphere of boundless consciousness, no perception of the sphere of nothingness in the sphere of nothingness, no perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, no perception of this world in this world, and no perception of the other world in the other world, yet he would still be perceiving?"
"There could be, friend Ānanda, such an attainment of concentration for a monk, in which he would have no perception of earth in earth... [list repeats] ...and no perception of the other world in the other world, yet he would still be perceiving."

2. "In what way, friend Sāriputta, could there be such an attainment of concentration for a monk...?"
"At one time, friend Ānanda, I was staying here in Sāvatthī in the Andha Grove. There, I entered such a concentration that I had no perception of earth in earth, no perception of water in water... [list repeats] ...I had no perception of this world in this world, and I had no perception of the other world in the other world, yet I was still perceiving."

3. "What was the Venerable Sāriputta's perception at that time?"
"The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna, the cessation of becoming is Nibbāna—thus, friend, a different perception arises in me, and a different perception ceases. Just as, friend, in a burning fire of twigs, one flame arises and another flame ceases, in the same way, friend, 'the cessation of becoming is Nibbāna, the cessation of becoming is Nibbāna'—a different perception arises and a different perception ceases, yet I was perceiving at that time, friend."

<summary>Sāriputta describes his own experience of this meditative state, using the analogy of a flame to explain the arising and ceasing of perceptions of Nibbāna.</summary>

to deceased relatives and blood kin. But, brahmin, is a giver ever fruitless? You might say, 'The recluse Gotama speaks of speculative consequences even in impossible situations.' Brahmin, I do indeed speak of speculative consequences in certain situations. Here, brahmin, a certain person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind filled with ill will, and holds wrong view. Yet, he is a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, fragrances, ointments, bedding, housing, and lights to a recluse or brahmin. Upon the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the company of elephants. There, he enjoys food, drink, and various garlands and ornaments. It is because he destroyed life and held wrong views that he is reborn in the company of elephants after the dissolution of his body upon death. But it is because he was a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, fragrances, ointments, bedding, housing, and lights to a recluse or brahmin that he enjoys food, drink, and various garlands and ornaments there.

Furthermore, brahmin, a certain person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind filled with ill will, and holds wrong view. 278. Tattha asamādinnasikkhāpadānam attano jātivayabāhusaccādīni paccavekkhitvā ayuttam. Amhākam evarūpam kātun ti sampattavatthum avītikkamantānam uppajjamānā virati sampattā virati ti veditabbā Sīhaladīpe Cakkaṇa-upāsakassa viya. Tassa kira daharakāle yeva mātuyā rogo uppajji vejjena ca allasamaṃsam laddhum vaṭṭati ti vuttam. Tato Cakkaṇassa bhātā ‘gaccha tāta, khettaṃ āhiṇḍā ti’ Cakkaṇaṃ pesesi. So tattha gato. Tasmiñ ca samaye eko saso taruṇassaṃ khāditum āgato hoti. So taṃ disvā vegena dhāvanto valliyā baddho kiri kiri ti saddam akāsi. Cakkaṇo tena saddena gantvā taṃ gahetvā cintesi ‘mātu bhesajjaṃ karomi ti’. Puna cintesi ‘na me taṃ paṭirūpaṃ mātu jīvitakāraṇena paraṃ jīvitā voropeyyan ti’. Atha naṃ ‘gaccha araññe sasehi saddhiṃ tiṇodakaṃ paribhuñjā ti’ muñci bhātarā ca ‘kiṃ tāta saso laddho ti’ pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Tato nam bhātā paribhāsi. So mātuyā santikaṃ gantvā ‘yato ‘ham jāto nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā ti’ saccaṃ vatvā aṭṭhāsi. Tāvad ev’assa mātā arogā ahosi¹.

279. Samādinna-sikkhāpadānaṃ pana sikkhāpadasamādāne tad uttariñ ca attano jīvitaṃ pi pariccajitvā vatthum avītikkamantānam uppajjamānā virati samādānaviratī ti veditabbā Uttaravaḍḍhamānavāsī-upāsakassa viya. So kira Ambariyavihāravāsī-Piṅgalabuddharakkhitattherassa santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā khettaṃ kasati. Tassa goṇo naṭṭho. So taṃ gavesanto Uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbataṃ āruhi. Tattha naṃ mahāsappo aggahesi. So cintesi ‘imāy’ assa tikhiṇavāsiyā sīsaṃ chindāmi ti’. Puna cintesi ‘na me taṃ paṭirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ bhāvaniyassa garuno santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā bhindeyyan ti’ evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ cintetvā ‘jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi na sikkhāpadaṃ ti’ amse ṭhapitaṃ tikhiṇaṃ daṇḍavāsiṃ araññe chaḍḍesi. Tāvad eva naṃ mahāvālo muñcitvā agamāsī ti².

<header>Atthasālinī 279.</header>

It is threefold: abstinence by concurrence, abstinence by undertaking, and abstinence by eradication.

278. In this context, regarding those who have not undertaken the precepts: when they consider their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, thinking, "It is not appropriate for one like me to do such a thing," and they experience abstinence while not overstepping the occasion, this should be understood as abstinence by concurrence. This is like the story of the lay-devotee Cakkaṇa in the island of Sri Lanka. It is said that in his youth, his mother fell ill, and the physician said that fresh meat was required [for her recovery]. Cakkaṇa's brother sent him out, saying, "Go, dear one, and roam the fields." He went there. At that time, a hare, having come to eat the young corn, saw him and, running swiftly, became caught in a vine, making a squealing sound. Cakkaṇa, having gone toward the sound and captured it, thought, "I will use this as medicine for my mother." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to take the life of another for the sake of my mother's life." Then he released it, saying, "Go, live in the forest with the other hares." When asked by his brother, "Dear one, did you catch a hare?" he told him the story. His brother scolded him. He went to his mother and stood there, saying, "Since I was born, I do not recall intentionally taking the life of any living being," declaring the truth. At that very moment, his mother became healthy.<note>Hardy Manual of Buddhism p. 480.</note>

279. As for abstinence by undertaking: for those who have taken the precepts, when abstinence arises while not overstepping the occasion, even at the cost of one's own life, having undertaken the precepts, this should be understood as abstinence by undertaking. This is like the story of the lay-devotee who lived in Uttaravaḍḍhamāna. It is said that he had taken the precepts from the elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita, who lived in the Ambariya monastery, and was plowing his field. His ox went missing. While searching for it, he climbed the Uttaravaḍḍhamāna mountain. There, a great serpent seized him. He thought, "I will cut off its head with this sharp wood-cutting tool." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to break the precepts I have taken in the presence of a venerable teacher who is worthy of cultivation." Having thought this up to the third time, he threw the sharp tool he had placed on his shoulder into the forest, saying, "I will abandon my life, but not my precept." At that very moment, the great serpent released him and departed.<note>Hardy Eastern Monachism p. 273.</note>

Tatra tatr’ eva sakkhibhabbatam pāpuṇāti sati sati āyatane ti ādīsu kāraṇaṃ.

Idha pana sañjātidesaṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhenā ti tividho pi vaṭṭati. Phassādayo hi dhammā ettha sañjāyanti ti sañjātidesaṭṭhena pi āyatanaṃ.

Bahiddhā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbārammaṇabhāve pan’ ettha osaranti ti samosaraṇaṭṭhanena pi āyatanaṃ, phassādīnaṃ pana sahajātādipaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇattā kāraṇaṭṭhena pi āyatanan ti veditabbaṃ.

Manindriyaṃ vuttattham eva.

Vijānātī ti viññāṇaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ eva khandho viññāṇakkhandho. Tassa rāsiādivasena attho veditabbo. ‘Mahādakakkhandho tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī ti’ ettha rāsaṭṭhena khandhajo vutto. Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho ti ādīsu guṇaṭṭhena. ‘Addasa kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhan ti’ ettha paññattimattaṭṭhena. Idha pana rūḷhito khandho vutto. Rāsaṭṭhena hi viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadeso ekaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tasmā yathā rukkhassa ekaṃ desaṃ chindanto ‘rukkhaṃ chindatī ti’ vuccati evam eva viññāṇakkhandhassa ekadesabhūtaṃ ekaṃ pi viññāṇaṃ rūḷhito viññāṇakkhandho ti vuttaṃ.

Tajjā manoviññāṇadhātū ti tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ anucchavikā manoviññāṇadhātu. Imasmim hi pade ekaṃ eva cittaṃ minanaṭṭhena mano, vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ, sabhāvaṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena vā dhātū ti tīhi nāmehi vuttaṃ.

...the base should be understood.

For example, in the world, in expressions like ‘lord-base’ or ‘Vasudeva-base,’ the dwelling place is called the base; in expressions like ‘gold-base’ or ‘jewel-base,’ it is an aspect. In the teaching, in ‘Birds frequent the pleasant base,’ it refers to a place of confluence; in ‘The south is the base for cattle,’ it refers to a place of origination. In ‘When the base exists, one attains the capacity for realization,’ it refers to a cause.

Here, all three are appropriate: in the sense of a place of origination, a place of confluence, and a place of cause. For the dhammas such as contact originate here, so it is a base in the sense of a place of origination.

Externally, the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch flow into it, so it is a base in the sense of a place of confluence. And because it is the cause for contact and the others by way of being a conascent condition, it should be understood as a base in the sense of a cause.

The faculty of mind is as already stated.

‘That which cognizes’ is consciousness. Consciousness itself as an aggregate is the consciousness-aggregate. Its meaning should be understood by way of the ‘heap’ and so on. In ‘The great mass of water attains the designation,’ ‘aggregate’ is used in the sense of a heap. In ‘aggregate of morality,’ ‘aggregate of concentration,’ etc., it is used in the sense of a quality. In ‘The Exalted One saw a great log of wood,’ it is used in the sense of a mere concept. Here, the aggregate is used in the sense of usage. For one part of the consciousness-aggregate, one single consciousness, is a heap in the sense of a mass. Therefore, just as one who cuts a part of a tree is said to be ‘cutting a tree,’ in the same way, even one single consciousness, being a part of the consciousness-aggregate, is called the consciousness-aggregate by usage.

‘The appropriate mental-consciousness element’—for those dhammas such as contact, the appropriate mental-consciousness element. For in this term, one and the same mind is called ‘mind’ in the sense of measuring, ‘consciousness’ in the sense of cognizing, and ‘element’ in the sense of own-nature or being void of a self; thus it is called by three names.

Thus, in this pentad of contact, contact is just that. Since contact is thus the appropriate mental-consciousness element born of contact, and so is the mind. Since the appropriate mental-consciousness element is thus, therefore in this...

Sāyam pana² navakatarehi attano upaṭṭhānam anāgatehi yeva tassa santikam gantvā nisīditvā avisaye apucchitvā tassa visaye pañho pucchitabbo. ‘Tumhe katarabhāṇakā ti’ apucchitvā ‘tumhākam ācariyūpajjhāyā kataram gantham valañjenti ti’ pucchitvā pahonakaṭṭhāne pañho pucchitabbo. Sace kathetum sakkoti icc’etam kusalam, no ce sakkoti sāyam kathetvā dātabbam. Evam ekadesena dhammapaṭisanthāro kato nāma hoti. Sace attano santike vasati³ tam ādāya nibaddham⁴ piṇḍāya caritabbam. Sace gantukāmo hoti punadivase gamanasabhāgena tam ādāya ekasmim gāme piṇḍāya caritvā uyyojetabbo.

Sace aññasmim disābhāge bhikkhū nimantitā honti tam bhikkhum icchamānam⁵ ādāya gantabbam. ‘Na mayham esā disā sabhāgā ti’ gantum anicchante sesabhikkhū pesetvā tam ādāya piṇḍāya caritabbam, attanā laddhāmisam tassa dātabbam. Evam āmisapaṭisanthāro kato nāma hoti. Āmisapaṭisanthārakena pana attanā laddham kassa dātabban ti? Āgantukassa tāva dātabbam. Sace gilāno vā avassiko vā atthi tesam pi dātabbam. Ācariyūpajjhāyānam dātabbam, bhaṇḍagāhakassa dātabbam. Sārāṇiyadhammapūrakena pana satavāram pi sahassavāram pi ābhatābhatena⁶ therāsanato paṭṭhāya dātabbam. Paṭisanthārakena pana yena yena laddham tassa tassa dātabbam. Bahi gāmam nikkhamitvā jiṇṇakam anātham vā bhikkhunim vā disvā tesam pi dātabbam.

Atthasālinī 829.

An alms-bowl and robe should be received, and a seat provided. One should fan him with a palm-leaf fan, wash his feet, and massage them. If there is ghee or molasses, medicine should be given; he should be asked if he has drinking water, and the residence should be attended to. In this way, a material welcome <term>āmisapaṭisanthāra</term> <gloss>welcome through physical provisions</gloss> is said to have been performed in part. As for the afternoon, if those who are junior have not come to attend to him, one should go into his presence, sit down, and without asking about matters outside his expertise, one should ask questions within his field of knowledge. Without asking, "To which reciters do you belong?" one should ask, "Which text do your teachers and preceptors use?" and then pose the question in a suitable place. If he is able to speak on it, this is excellent; if he is not able, one should speak on it oneself and provide the information. In this way, a welcome through the Dhamma <term>dhammapaṭisanthāra</term> <gloss>welcome through spiritual teaching</gloss> is said to have been performed in part. If he resides in one’s own quarters, one should take him along and go regularly for alms. If he wishes to depart, on the next day, one should take him along to a village on the way, go for alms, and then see him off.

If monks have been invited in another direction, one should go taking the monk along if he wishes to go. If he does not wish to go, saying, "That direction is not suitable for me," one should send the remaining monks, go for alms taking him along, and give him the alms one has obtained. In this way, a material welcome is said to have been performed. To whom should that which is obtained by one performing a material welcome be given? First, it should be given to the newcomer. If there is a sick person or one who is on a temporary stay, it should be given to them as well. It should be given to teachers and preceptors, and it should be given to the storekeeper. However, by one fulfilling the qualities of cordiality <term>sārāṇiyadhamma</term> <gloss>states of conciliation</gloss>, it should be given starting from the seat of the Elder, even if it has been brought again and again a hundred or a thousand times. But by one performing a welcome, it should be given to whoever it was obtained for. Having gone outside the village, if one sees an elderly or helpless monk or nun, it should be given to them as well.

829. Regarding this, there is this story: It is said that when Guttasālā was attacked by thieves, at that very moment, an Elder nun who had arisen from the cessation of perception and feeling <term>nirodha</term> <gloss>a meditative attainment</gloss> had a young nun take her belongings, and having set out on the road with the great crowd, at high noon [she reached] Nakulana-

<summary>This passage details the specific monastic protocols for welcoming and assisting visiting monks, distinguishing between physical provisions and spiritual hospitality, while emphasizing the priority of care for the sick, the elderly, and the helpless.</summary>

liberated through right knowledge, has lifted the bar, filled in the moat, drawn up the stake, is without obstruction, a noble one, with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached, completely victorious, whose suffering is fully understood, whose origin is abandoned, whose cessation is realized, whose path is developed, whose object to be known is known, whose object to be understood is understood, whose object to be abandoned is abandoned, whose object to be developed is developed, whose object to be realized is realized, and does the temporary-liberated Arahant fall away from Arahant-ship?
Yes.
Is the untemporary-liberated Arahant free from passion, free from hatred—[etc.]—whose object to be realized is realized, and does the untemporary-liberated Arahant fall away from Arahant-ship?
It should not be said so.

Yes.

It should not be said so.
Is hatred abandoned for an untemporary-liberated Arahant—[etc.]—is lack of moral shame abandoned, and does the untemporary-liberated Arahant not fall away from Arahant-ship?
Yes.
Is lack of moral shame abandoned for a temporary-liberated Arahant, and does the temporary-liberated Arahant not fall away from Arahant-ship?
It should not be said so.
53. Is the path developed for an untemporary-liberated Arahant for the abandoning of passion—[etc.]—have the limbs of enlightenment been developed, and does the untemporary-liberated Arahant not fall away from Arahant-ship?
Yes.
Is the path developed for a temporary-liberated Arahant for the abandoning of passion—[etc.]—have the limbs of enlightenment been developed, and does the temporary-liberated Arahant not fall away from Arahant-ship?
It should not be said so.
Is the path developed for an untemporary-liberated Arahant for the abandoning of hatred—[etc.]—for the abandoning of lack of moral shame—have the limbs of enlightenment been developed, and does the untemporary-liberated Arahant not fall away from Arahant-ship?
Yes.

Āmantā.

Āmantā.

Yes.

It should not be said—and so on—

Yes.

Yes.

Yes.

It should not be said—and so on—

Yes.

Yes.

then it must be said that "the aggregate of consciousness is associated with the aggregate of mental formations."
Just as oil is permeated and entered into sesame seeds, and as juice is permeated and entered into sugarcane, are these phenomena permeated and entered into those phenomena?
It should not be said so—[etcetera]—

VII. 3.

1. Is there no such thing as a mental phenomenon?
Yes.
But are there not some phenomena that are concomitant with the mind, born together, mutually intertwined, associated, having the same arising, the same cessation, the same base, and the same object?
Yes.
If there are some phenomena that are concomitant with the mind, born together, mutually intertwined, associated, having the same arising, the same cessation, the same base, and the same object, then it should not be said that "there is no such thing as a mental phenomenon."
2. Is contact born together with the mind?
Yes.
If contact is born together with the mind, then it must be said that "contact is a mental phenomenon."
Are feeling—[etcetera]—perception, volition—[etcetera]—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, greed, hatred, delusion—[etcetera]—lack of conscience born together with the mind?
Yes.
If lack of conscience is born together with the mind, then it must be said that "lack of conscience is a mental phenomenon."
3. Are they called mental phenomena because they are born together with the mind?
Yes.
Are they called "contact-phenomena" because they are born together with contact?
Yes.
Are they called mental phenomena because they are born together with the mind?

- **ענן** ישכננו בדמים כככה ספ' שישיה מתעכבת מכל וב' חסיד ישתעף ויתלה ויכרה לפי המקום ולפי הזמן וכמו שבדלקין במלקוס שהיה עולה ליתן הס' מלכמה שלום הן במנשר בימור בסס כחסלו סעי ללית דוק מליליס סוס :
- **ענף עץ עבות** קול קסד וסקס והלכה ב' י' ה' הדרכה מכל הסד הבדה בנב (שבבע ענב הבור סוד ו' י' ספירות סבמיכה ולכן נקרא ענף עבות בבור ד'י וקיה תולדות קסד' כערכו :
- **עפר** סוד הקסס מדת המלכות ובסס' סירה בס' גדוליס גמילה סד"ה קדס ענף על עבות ולכן נקרס עפר סבשלה בדס' לס סלסה וירדו לדעת כי באשר נשדשר ענף עץ עבות קס הסנדליס קס קיו סלמה וכל סס סמס בכדסה' א' ולכן בריך ג' בדי סדי קדס וקנה בזה בחר קיסה דרמז סל סדקת סס פו' פגלו סיקס ויקל העכן וקול בס"מ סבדרר דוהר ומקיבה בס' ובי מיחה בזהר ויקל וכן מה ביחה הבקר :
- **עץ** סוד מדת המלכות ונקראה עבד כי בו נוס סיסו סל ספירות וכו' בסדיוס בבחינת קדומיס וקו קול עוסה פירות כמו סנדבר בערך פירות וקן בסדו דובר ד סקוה וכו' פו' מי עבי' עבד ג' בבביס ובזהר פ' בס' ובפ' חלק בסהמה מי מנא עמי וקו' קדבוס כי בסר סס בקבה חיין סדר נבקה בסוד סזיל ס' ססיה הבעדא הקיה וסקל וק' פו' ק' המבקה יחד פקוא קדן הקדק וכן חותה בובות שיין קם דקסד בבחינה הקסקגה קן במנקר סס יס' פ' בסור בחיבה זו קדרה המבקה עבד ובענבל הנריס קם ב' כי קקדמות נקרס עפר בבית יקיקה סס סס' ג' ספירות והדס עופר במנקר סדווקא בעת הגבירה בל הדבוס ק' :
- **עץ החיים וכו'** סלעס עליס קס סס במנקר סדיס ען סקיס קו'ק' ס סלכה סס דמיס במיעין וסבד פלו כי סחיים וסקסס בו קער סקוס סס ססירות בבדל ונקרה קיים וקיים סכתה ען וקו' נזבר במקומו לביס בסדר בס'ד' ס' פ' סקיים ס"ק מסיק לילה ססבל מעסה וניק וכן פילה קדבסיס ופוד בססר סקוא מסדר ק'ק פלוס פ' ובסמה ס' פ' בססר מעבר ועבר מעבר סס ק' ומוסד נדרס עץ קסדד לפי סקו' המיבות וסגן בכה נקרס ע'ן קסד בסד סר' ובר ססירס בסס' וסד מרבי סלמלתה לבר הבחינה סיומה בדורה פנימי סספירות וסדקייס בסס ומקרסיס בסס ' בו בסיכון סח' ויס ען קרי וקיה המלכות ונקרה פץ פדי מפי פקיס קורדבי ופי סס וקחיות קספינס סהעככסה וקס בס' סבנקר בזהר פ' וס' וס' עץ סדעת טוב ורע דבעס"ק פודס קדב"ס פ'ע'ס' בססרי' המלכות עץ סדעת טוב ורע וחין דקסחפק ודוהר המלכות יש בה דט ק"ו פי' סס, דס מובקר בס מפי סמקינה סוס ודע דמקס בף סדעת טוב ורע וסני פסק קקין בד דע בדד כמו סבסדסו בספר סס'ס' וקיים בס עיין דדך סיייסה סמלכות ולדסבות ובורד וסיס סס זה המבנה דמכס סק"ס סקוא יוצא מעדן סס ופס"ד דע' מס נדוד וגב' ובהחבד בזהר פדס' קדס בדדס'יה ויס עץ סקוא ועץ במזד פדס' קוס קדסד' דספ"ס' דחיות פיל סיוכא מפהמ' בסד וסקר פן סססירס סקן פבוס וביסו בענסיס כי בסד דאמר אד סמדבות וקבד דבודא קוא ענין ס' וס קורה בספירה :
- **עצב ועצבון** בסדו קודס בדס"י פסי סס בדיס פמבון בגיס וקבובה בדס סדורה ודמבין בד קמבדרסה קודרה ובבבי דא משחכסן וכו' בעבבון בבדס דדוקא דקיק דבמבע קלמבון המדה די שמקה וסבימ' כי וסבס' סדה בחיבה ססד סדוד וקססס פפביון וקדדו וכו' וסיין קסקסבה ויקדי לו קדס סדבין :
- **עצה** פיהו דבקיבו ד"ו ביין הבמות ובבוובה כי בס וקוא בסס בסדיס בדסידבה

<column-break/>

- **על כל מים** הוא הבינה הק' כנודע סודם ושלח וכמ' ומכאן לק' מבני שלום על כל מים בסוד עימום ושלח למלכה מלכי כלו' וחסו' למעלה ממס'
- **עלות העולות** כחשמו דשער הק' שאין סוף הוא הכתר ויש חילוק בין עלת העלות ובין עלת כל העלות והם סוד באלהיו :
- **עמודי האש והענן** הם הבינה והתפארת ויצחק משקל בסוד מדת יום ולילה הק' כחס' עמ"ש הענ"ן כי ענן מכל המדה והשלהבת יוצא מגבורה ויצחק מדה כנגדס לכן לא נכלה עמוד הענן בלילה והתלה עמוד האש היום לא נכלה כי הם כבדים עם שמח גדיהם הוא הזוהר שהפסיק עמוד הענן והוא הם היו בעומדים נטש נטש בבית המקדש והיתה היו בכת' ועמוד והוא וכו' בקרדיס גם הם הם העמודים :
- **עמדי נקי** הקדר שהוא האצבעוניות :
- **ענבים** בבינה הם ו' ספירות והן קטנות וכנה שיין חומר מטפה ייין שראשית והם העת היזם יקרא ולאמ"ש יש ענבים לכל' ויש ענבי' שלומיס ויש ענביס מרורים הנזכרו בשאר וגם יש בע' שם הם ורב קלוס הזורה מורה על הק' ובססס כונקים הכבדים הם אדומי' ואם נפסק יהיו קור לו שהסכינו שתיקנוהו ובכלו והשקומ' פירוש פז' השקיבהו משאר הדרת הרגי' בו פירס דכלי הטייס השכוכ' ונפסק קסס בס' כי הענבים הם בחלקין והשמר השפע הטעין כי הענבים אביו לקו הם של קלוס האשכנז ומחזקה בהם שיין העתיק השפע הם אין ביה וכס' וקין נוח והיינו שירקינו שיה בין קדושי' לדרכי' :
- **ענני** ענני קודש שבהמ"ש עם שין בי'כנ' ובסקה' בבא פירס בשנ"ק ומבקה' ויסח המכין לבי
- **עננה** תיבות "ענ"י" "גב" "ני" פילס על י' בינה סס חכמה וסתר השכל עכ' י' כסד שלמלה שהוא הכסד היוצא מבינה ומקשה הגן שהוא המלכות וכל זה שלמו בשינה כב'כ' ש. והנה מוהר לומר כי שי' עננה והשגלו הוד בבינה והתבינה על ה'. דיויתה דקינו בינה ואפשר לומר כי שבינה נקרא עננ' שהיה בעולס השובה הק' ב'
- **עני** פי' הק'מ דמות השפע המפעל הללו מדרשכחן ענ' הם משה רבינו עליו השלום והנו באשר ובפוק' משה עניו מכל ומ' ד"ז ל' מט דעעמה התה במפה בחמה ליקשה פטמה ענוה עקן לסבינה פי' כי המלכוס נקראת יראה מצד המלך והשחמה בחמה מכל הימיין וחסיה מגבורה המללה על סי' סין קורה לכן לאחד בחמה יראה ה' כי לבינה קילקה הלה מכל הדשה זה וה' ענף ועשה ובכל בחשע והקשר עניו בחור קדשת וחסידות שהי' לשמעיה עברת בעולד לכן אמרו שחסיבות ענוה היא עבירה לעולם עליה והיינו בסור ענוה הסור באשר :

# Gate 22: The Gate of the Values of Epithets, Chapter 16

<column-break/>

<margin>Cloud</margin>
- **Cloud** <note>original: Anan</note>
He dwells within the <unclear>bloods</unclear>. This is how the sixth Sephirah <note>Tiferet</note> is delayed from all. The "Pious One" will branch out, be suspended, and be dug according to the place and time. Just as in the flickering of the <term>malkosh</term> <gloss>late rain</gloss> which would rise to give the secret of many kinds of peace.

<margin>Bough of Thick Trees</margin>
- **Bough of Thick Trees** <note>original: Anaf Etz Avot</note>
This is <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss>. The numerical value is 15. It is the guidance from all of the <term>Chesed</term>. It is the secret of the six Sefirot in their connection. Therefore, it is called a "thick bough" because of the connection of the <term>Yod</term> <gloss>the letter Y</gloss> and the <term>Heh</term> <gloss>the letter H</gloss>, which are the offspring of <term>Chesed</term> in its value.

<margin>Dust</margin>
- **Dust** <note>original: Afar</note>
The secret of the attribute of <term>Malchut</term> <gloss>Kingship</gloss>. This is explained in the collections on the great books regarding the "Bough of Thick Trees." It is called "Dust" because it was created in the likeness of the <unclear>man</unclear>. They descended to know that when the "Bough of Thick Trees" was rooted, these were the <term>Sandalim</term> <gloss>foundations or angelic levels</gloss>. All of them were complete in one holiness. Therefore, it is blessed in the secret of the holy field.

<margin>Tree</margin>
- **Tree** <note>original: Etz</note>
The secret of the attribute of <term>Malchut</term> <gloss>Kingship</gloss>. It is called a "servant" because in it is the <term>Yesod</term> <gloss>Foundation</gloss> of the Sefirot. It refers to the ancient aspects. It produces fruit, as discussed in the entry for **Fruit**. This refers to the secret of "Who makes a tree." It is found in the Zohar and in the section of <term>Chelek</term> <gloss>portion</gloss> regarding the question of "Who is the master of the house?" This refers to the ancient ones because there the King of Life is found. It is the secret of the female aspect. It is the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. In the aspect of the lower world, it is the mystery of the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>.

<margin>Tree of Life etc.</margin>
- **Tree of Life etc.** <note>original: Etz HaChayim</note>
The leaves are there in the source. The Tree of Life is the <term>Vav</term> <gloss>the sixth letter, representing Tiferet</gloss>. It goes as water in the intestines. Life and the attribute of the Sefirot are contained within it. It is called "Life" because it sustains the Tree. It is mentioned in its place in the Zohar regarding the secret of the night and the deed. Also, it is the secret of the "Garden." It is called the "Tree of Chesed" according to the attributes. This is the inner aspect of the Sefirot. There is also a "Fruit Tree," which is <term>Malchut</term>. It is called a "Fruit Tree" because it receives from the celestial tree. In the Zohar, it is called the "Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil." Know that the <term>Malchut</term> <gloss>Kingship</gloss> contains both Good and Evil. Good comes from the side of holiness, and Evil from the side of the shell. As explained in the book of the <term>Hechalot</term> <gloss>Palaces</gloss>, this structure comes out of Eden. The Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil is the secret of the souls that go out from there.

<margin>Sorrow and Pain</margin>
- **Sorrow and Pain** <note>original: Atzev v'Itzavon</note>
This is the secret of the garments. "Pain" refers to the body and the form. In the Zohar it says that in "pain" <note>itzavon</note> refers to the male side. Specifically, it is the sadness of the attribute that is not joyful. This is the aspect of judgment and the secret of the "Garment of Skin."

<margin>Counsel</margin>
- **Counsel** <note>original: Etzah</note>
Its meaning is the connection of the <term>Vav</term> and the <term>Heh</term> <gloss>the last two letters of the Divine Name</gloss> through <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Upon all Waters</margin>
- **Upon all Waters** <note>original: Al Kol Mayim</note>
This is the holy <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>, as is known from before. It is the secret of the "Peaceful ones who dwell upon all waters." It refers to the concealment and the sending of the Queen to her King. It is above the measured levels.

<margin>Cause of Causes</margin>
- **Cause of Causes** <note>original: Alat HaAlot</note>
This is the secret of the holy gate. The Infinite <note>Ein Sof</note> is the <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss>. There is a difference between the "Cause of Causes" and the "Cause of All Causes." They are the secret of the Divinity.

<margin>Pillars of Fire and Cloud</margin>
- **Pillars of Fire and Cloud** <note>original: Amudei HaEsh veHaAnan</note>
These are <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss> and <term>Tiferet</term> <gloss>Beauty</gloss>. Isaac represents the weight of the secret of the attribute of day and night. The cloud comes from the attribute and the flame goes out from <term>Gevurah</term> <gloss>Severity</gloss>. Isaac is the corresponding attribute. Therefore, the pillar of cloud did not depart by night, nor the pillar of fire by day. They are heavy with their greatness. It is the brilliance that separates the pillar of cloud. They were the ones standing in the Holy Temple.

<margin>Clean Hands</margin>
- **Clean Hands** <note>original: Imdi Naki</note>
The <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss>, which is like the fingers.

<margin>Grapes</margin>
- **Grapes** <note>original: Anavim</note>
In <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>, they are the six Sefirot. They are small. They are the matter of the initial drop. They are the time of the day. There are "Grapes for the Bride," "Whole Grapes," and "Bitter Grapes" mentioned in other gates. Also, the abundance that flows from the holiness. If they are red, it indicates the attribute of judgment. If they are harvested, it indicates they have been rectified.

<margin>Answer me</margin>
- **Answer me** <note>original: Aneni</note>
Holy responses in the Temple with the Divine Name. It refers to the preparation of the heart.

<margin>Cloudiness</margin>
- **Cloudiness** <note>original: Ananah</note>
The letters of "Ani" <gloss>Poor/I</gloss> and "Gan" <gloss>Garden</gloss>. It refers to the <term>Yod</term> of <term>Binah</term>, which contains <term>Chochmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss> and <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss> of the intellect. It is the <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> that goes out from <term>Binah</term> and waters the Garden, which is the <term>Malchut</term> <gloss>Kingship</gloss>. This is achieved through the secret of <term>Binah</term>.

<margin>Poor / Humble</margin>
- **Poor** <note>original: Ani</note>
The secret of the attribute where the flow of abundance is processed. Our master Moses, peace be upon him, was "humble" <note>anav</note> more than any man. This is the secret of the attribute of Wisdom. Humility is a heel to Wisdom. This means that <term>Malchut</term> is called "Fear" from the side of the King. Wisdom is above all. Humility is the bond of holiness and piety. Therefore, they said that humility is the greatest of all virtues.

<margin>Poor (man/woman)</margin>
- **Poor** <note>original: Ani</note>
There is a "Poor man" <note>Ani</note> and a "Poor woman" <note>Aniyah</note>. The poor man is the seeker. As Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said, "he who has nothing of his own." This refers to the <term>Malchut</term> which has no light of its own, like the moon. It receives everything from the Sefirot above it. It is like a garment. The Sefira itself is hidden behind the glass. The reason it is called "poor" is so that the will of man can be tested through it. It is through his counsel and for the sake of the Name.
